item.title: Jax Morning Brief — DHS Raids Omar's Home, Obama Speaks Out, Russia Sanctions Reversed
item.description: DHS searched Rep. Ilhan Omar's home as the administration moves to strip her citizenship, drawing a rare rebuke from Obama. Plus, Trump waives Russia sanctions over GOP objections, and Anthropic's borrowing costs spike ahead of its unfiled IPO.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning, and welcome back from the weekend. It's Monday, October 19th, 2026. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: Federal agents searched the home of Congresswoman Ilhan Omar this weekend as the administration moves to strip her citizenship, and former President Obama weighed in directly. We'll get into that.

ANDREW: And over the weekend, Anthropic agreed to pay a double-digit interest rate to borrow billions of dollars, right as its long-awaited IPO filing is still nowhere to be found. We'll explain why that matters.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed Friday at 7,659, down about 1.1 percent. The Dow finished at 52,002, down a more modest 0.3 percent. The Nasdaq took the hardest hit, closing at 26,140, down 2.1 percent. For the week, the S and P and the Nasdaq both posted their worst stretch since June, as a sharp selloff in AI and chip stocks spread through the market. The ten-year Treasury yield sits around 5.07 percent, and the thirty-year fixed mortgage rate is holding at 7.40 percent, according to Freddie Mac.

ANDREW: Here's the weekend at a glance. A hotter than expected inflation report on wholesale prices, up 1.3 percent for the month, the biggest jump since March of 2022, combined with that chip and AI stock selloff, dragged markets down hard last week. Futures are pointing to a bounce back this morning, with oil prices and yields easing, but the Fed is now in its pre-meeting quiet period ahead of a decision next week that could set the tone for the rest of the year.

ANDREW: Let's start with the biggest story of the weekend. DHS agents searched Congresswoman Ilhan Omar's home in Washington, as part of an investigation that the Wall Street Journal reports is aimed at stripping her citizenship and deporting her.

JENNY: Wait, deporting a sitting member of Congress? What's the actual allegation here?

ANDREW: The claim, led out of the U.S. Attorney's office, is that Omar or her late father falsified naturalization paperwork back in the early 2000s, including her birth date. ICE director Tom Homan says investigators believe they have a strong case. No charges have been filed against Omar or anyone else at this point, and her reelection is just a few weeks away, on November 3rd.

JENNY: So this is still an investigation, not an indictment.

ANDREW: Correct, and that distinction matters. What's new since Friday is that former President Obama issued a public statement Sunday calling the effort a transparent attempt at intimidation. It's his first major political intervention of the year, and it signals how far this story has traveled beyond Minneapolis politics.

JENNY: It's rare for a former president to weigh in this directly on an active investigation.

ANDREW: It is, which is exactly why the administration's framing of this as a routine paperwork case is running into trouble. Expect this one to keep escalating as her reelection gets closer.

ANDREW: The other major story out of Washington this weekend: President Trump waived a new round of sanctions on Russia just two days before they were set to take effect, the second such waiver in two weeks. The move is tied to an effort to ease diesel and oil prices, but it's drawn open criticism from Senate Republicans, including Mitch McConnell, Thom Tillis, Susan Collins, and John Cornyn, all of whom are urging him to reverse course.

JENNY: That's striking, a president overriding sanctions that his own party passed into law.

ANDREW: It is, and it's landed in the middle of an already tense relationship with Ukraine's Zelenskyy, who has separately accused the U.S. of throttling Starlink speeds for Ukrainian forces. Treasury Secretary Bessent pushed back on that claim publicly over the weekend.

ANDREW: Overseas, the Iran and Saudi conflict remains unresolved. Iran's Revolutionary Guard claims two more tankers struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend, though there's no independent confirmation of that yet, so treat it as Iran's claim for now. Iran's foreign ministry says a seven day proposal to reopen the strait is still on the table through Qatar, but the U.S. hasn't accepted it. Oil prices are elevated, roughly 105 to 110 dollars a barrel for Brent crude, and shipping through the strait remains well below normal, with daily volumes down to an estimated 11 to 12 million barrels a day, versus a baseline of around 17 million before the war started, according to the Energy Information Administration. President Trump has repeated that there will be no U.S. strikes before the November 3rd midterms.

ANDREW: And one more thread to watch out of Washington: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh spoke in Bangkok Friday and declined to preview next week's rate decision. Markets now put the odds of a hike at around 14 to 15 percent, down further from last week, and Goldman Sachs is now forecasting a pause this month with one more hike in December.

JENNY: That's a pretty big swing from where things stood just a couple weeks ago.

ANDREW: It is. Hike odds briefly topped 50 percent after that hot September inflation report, so this is a real shift in how the market expects the Fed to read the data.

ANDREW: Jenny, let's head down to Jacksonville.

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a high near 71 degrees today, mostly sunny but breezy, with winds gusting up to 27 miles an hour. There's a gale warning in effect for coastal waters through tonight, so it's not a great day to be out on the water, but a nice one on land before temperatures cool into the upper 50s tonight.

JENNY: The biggest local story this weekend involves Mayor Donna Deegan directly. The Florida Attorney General's Office of Statewide Prosecution has personally subpoenaed her, and she has until tomorrow, October 20th, to comply.

ANDREW: What exactly are they after?

JENNY: Records and communications tied to a March 2025 meeting between Deegan and a former JTA board member named Megan Hayward, who says she raised alarms about the transit authority's finances well before the crisis became public. It's separate from the subpoena already outstanding to JTA itself, due October 30th, which seeks records involving current JTA leader Cleveland Ferguson, former CEO Nat Ford, and Deegan. All of this stems from the thirty-nine million dollar budget shortfall that forced City Council to approve tapping up to thirty million dollars in gas tax funds back on October 13th.

ANDREW: So the question now is what Deegan knew, and when.

JENNY: Exactly, and we'll know more once her deadline passes tomorrow.

JENNY: Separately, the downtown Publix tower project, known as Pearl Square, remains in limbo. City Council President Nick Howland says the council wants to see how the November 3rd Amendment 3 vote turns out before committing to the incentive package, because the council's own auditor projects that amendment could cut city revenue by two hundred million dollars in the next fiscal year alone, and three hundred million the year after.

ANDREW: Remind us what's actually in that incentive package.

JENNY: It's just under fifty million dollars total, split between a twenty one million dollar tax rebate grant paid out over seventeen years and a twenty eight million dollar upfront completion grant, for a hundred forty million dollar development with a Publix, apartments, and parking. The Finance Committee vote is now set for November 4th, the day after the election, with a full council vote to follow on November 10th if it clears committee.

JENNY: And some good news on the sports front. Jaguars president Mark Lamping said this weekend the team wants to play its entire 2028 home schedule right here in Jacksonville, timed to the reopening of the renovated stadium. That would likely end the team's annual trip to London, which has run since 2013.

ANDREW: After all those years of splitting home games between here, Orlando, and London, that would be a nice change for season ticket holders. What's the timeline on the stadium itself?

JENNY: The one point four billion dollar renovation is still on track to finish in August of 2028. This season, the Jaguars are only playing six home games here in Jacksonville, with the rest split between Orlando and, as of yesterday, London, where they just played the Texans at Wembley.

JENNY: Andrew, what's happening on the mortgage side this week?

ANDREW: Rates were essentially flat to slightly lower over the past week. Freddie Mac's weekly survey held at 7.40 percent for a second straight week, while Mortgage News Daily's daily index closed Friday around 7.37 percent, down from highs earlier in the month. The Mortgage Bankers Association's own survey, though, showed the contract rate climbing to 7.50 percent for the week ending October 9th, the highest since November of 2023, and applications fell 2.7 percent as a result.

JENNY: So depending on which measure you look at, rates are either holding steady or near a two year high?

ANDREW: Both are true at once, which tells you we're in a choppy stretch. The bigger regulatory story is one we've been tracking for a week now: FHFA Director Bill Pulte was expected to announce a shift from pulling three credit bureau reports to just two for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac loans. He skipped the mortgage industry's own national conference in Chicago to attend a campaign event instead, and as of this morning, no formal announcement has been made. It remains under consideration, not policy.

JENNY: What would that change actually mean for someone applying for a mortgage?

ANDREW: In theory, a cheaper, faster underwriting process, since credit reports are a real cost in every loan. But without a formal rule, lenders are still operating under the old three bureau standard. One piece of actual movement came out of HUD on Friday: a new mortgagee letter opens FHA backed financing to build to rent communities, for the first time letting single family and small multifamily rental developments tap the same federal mortgage insurance that's long been reserved for traditional apartment buildings.

JENNY: That's a meaningful shift for an industry that's been building a lot of single family rentals.

ANDREW: It is, and it's worth watching whether other agencies follow HUD's lead. Beyond that, it was a quiet weekend for the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, no new fair lending actions or rule changes to flag, though the bureau is still expected to finalize changes to its streamlined refinance rules for Fannie and Freddie loans sometime this year.

ANDREW: Jenny, you've got some AI news for us too.

JENNY: I do, and it starts with Anthropic. The Financial Times reports the company is offering a double digit interest rate, over 10 percent, to borrowers backing a nine billion dollar slice of a sixty billion dollar financing package with Broadcom, money that would lock in access to Google's AI chips for the next five years.

ANDREW: Ten percent is a steep rate for a company this size. What were they paying before?

JENNY: Around 8.5 percent, just four months ago. That jump is a real signal that the cost of financing AI infrastructure is rising fast. And it lands at an awkward moment, because Anthropic's IPO paperwork still hasn't shown up. As of this morning, there's no public filing on the SEC's system, more than four months after the company first submitted its draft registration confidentially back in June. Analysts still expect a public filing around October 23rd, but that's their estimate, not a confirmed date from the company.

JENNY: There's also a broader trend worth flagging: major companies are starting to lock AI shopping and task agents out of their platforms. The Verge reports Amazon, Yelp, Delta, JPMorgan Chase, and Charles Schwab have all restricted outside AI agents, like Meta's Muse or OpenAI's newer agent tools, from completing real transactions on their sites. Schwab's CEO put it plainly: they're not ready to let an AI agent touch a customer's brokerage account.

ANDREW: That's a pretty direct response to how fast agentic AI tools have been moving this year.

JENNY: It is, and it's a story we'll likely keep following as more companies draw that same line. On top of that, the FTC's investigation into OpenAI and Anthropic's safety claims, which we told you about last week, is still active, with Politico reporting that Anthropic has quietly pitched Congress on a narrow bill that would let only a federal judge halt a frontier AI model, and only in the most extreme cases.

ANDREW: And didn't a Replit executive say something about dropping Anthropic entirely?

JENNY: He did, onstage at a conference last week, saying Replit's coding tool now defaults to OpenAI's models over cost and performance. But people close to the deal told TechCrunch the Anthropic partnership is actually still active behind the scenes, so take that one as a dispute between the two companies rather than a settled fact.

JENNY: That's it from the tech desk.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch this week: the Fed's two day policy meeting wraps up Wednesday, October 28th. Futures markets currently put the odds of a rate hike at only around one in six, and Goldman Sachs is now betting on a pause this month with one more hike in December. Watch whether Chair Warsh's language next week opens the door to that call. It's the single biggest swing factor for where mortgage rates and markets head into November.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Monday. Have a great start to your week.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Hot CPI Print Rattles Markets, OpenAI Engineer Arrested in Spy Case
item.description: A hotter-than-expected inflation report triggers Wall Street's worst selloff since July and scrambles Fed rate-hike odds. Plus, an OpenAI engineer is arrested for alleged espionage, and JTA's subpoena reaches the mayor's office.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Thursday, October 15th, 2026. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: A hotter than expected inflation report just triggered Wall Street's worst selloff since the summer and scrambled the odds of a Federal Reserve rate hike later this month.

ANDREW: And the FBI arrested an OpenAI engineer accused of planting a hidden recording device in the company's executive offices — we'll get into what he was allegedly after.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed down about 1.1 percent yesterday, at 7,718. The Dow held up better, down just a tenth of a percent. The Nasdaq dropped almost 2 percent as tech and AI-linked stocks took the brunt of the selling — Wall Street's worst session since July. The ten year Treasury yield eased to about 5.1 percent, down 9 basis points, and the thirty year fixed mortgage rate is tracking in the mid 7.40s according to Mortgage News Daily. We'll unpack what's actually driving all of this in a moment.

ANDREW: Let's start with what's moving those markets, because it goes back to yesterday morning.

ANDREW: The Labor Department's September inflation report came in hotter than economists expected. Headline consumer prices rose 3.7 percent from a year ago, and 0.6 percent in the month of September alone — above the 3.6 percent forecast. Core inflation, which strips out food and energy, climbed 2.6 percent annually. Gasoline prices, up 9.1 percent for the month, drove more than half of that increase.

JENNY: So walk me through why one report moved markets this much.

ANDREW: Because it reshapes the bet on what the Fed does at its October 28th meeting. Going into yesterday, traders priced the odds of an October hike at around 21 percent. After the report, those odds spiked above 50 percent before settling back near 37 percent. San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly struck a hawkish tone, saying more hikes are likely, though she wants the timing to stay deliberate. Fed Vice Chair Michelle Bowman pushed the other way, signaling a more cautious wait and see approach.

JENNY: That's a pretty public split for two Fed officials to be airing days before a big decision.

ANDREW: It is, and that's exactly why everyone will be watching Fed Chair Kevin Warsh closely today. He has a fireside chat scheduled in Bangkok with the IMF's Kristalina Georgieva — his first public remarks since the inflation number landed.

JENNY: And for someone just paying bills, what does a report like this actually change?

ANDREW: Mostly it means borrowing stays expensive a little longer. If the Fed leans toward another hike instead of holding steady, credit cards, auto loans, and the mortgage rates we'll get to shortly all take longer to come down. Gas and grocery prices are also still running ahead of wages for a lot of households, which is exactly why this single report carried so much weight in the markets yesterday.

ANDREW: Overseas, the Saudi-Houthi conflict kept escalating overnight. Houthi forces claimed new strikes on Riyadh's airport, a Saudi Aramco facility, and a refinery — claims Saudi officials haven't confirmed. What is confirmed, by Al Jazeera and Al Arabiya, is that the Saudi-led coalition intercepted a separate ballistic missile aimed at Riyadh, and falling debris injured at least four people. President Trump still hasn't committed any American forces, instead floating the idea that Turkey's Erdogan could step in to mediate on Saudi Arabia's behalf. Oil prices actually eased on the news, with Brent crude slipping to around 103 dollars a barrel.

JENNY: Still no sign of this cooling down on its own.

ANDREW: Not yet.

ANDREW: And here at home, the investigation into Congresswoman Ilhan Omar escalated. The Justice Department issued roughly a dozen subpoenas to her family members as part of a federal grand jury probe out of Minnesota, and agents seized her phone, computer, and passport during Sunday's home search. A judge has since limited how much of her records prosecutors can access. No charges have been filed against her or anyone else at this point.

ANDREW: One more from the national desk. The Justice Department's antitrust investigation into the broadcast networks over their joint suspension of pooled White House coverage hasn't produced any new charges or subpoenas, but Semafor reported yesterday, in a story not yet matched by a second outlet, that the White House played a central role in instigating the probe in the first place. Separately, two former Justice Department officials told CNBC they think the case has real First Amendment problems. No network has filed a formal response yet.

ANDREW: Jenny, you've got an even stranger federal case over on your beat this morning.

JENNY: It really is stranger. The FBI arrested an OpenAI engineer named Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national who'd been with the company since last July. Prosecutors say he hid a recording device inside a toilet paper roll in an executive conference room, installed in late September, specifically to capture conversations about OpenAI's advanced superintelligence research. A second device turned up in his bag.

ANDREW: Wait — a recording device hidden in a bathroom supply?

JENNY: In the toilet paper roll, in the conference room, yes. FBI Director Kash Patel confirmed the arrest on the record. OpenAI says so far there's no evidence any model code, weights, or customer data actually got out, and they've fired him.

ANDREW: Any sense yet of who he might have been working for?

JENNY: Nothing confirmed publicly yet — that's the piece everyone wants answered next.

JENNY: Meanwhile, Anthropic held the investor day we'd been watching for, and the numbers it shared were striking. Third quarter revenue came in at 16.8 billion dollars, up 45 percent from the quarter before, and the company says it's now adjusted profitable and cash flow positive, generating a dollar seventy in revenue for every dollar it spends on computing power. That's according to the Financial Times, Reuters, and Bloomberg, all citing people who attended. Bankers are still floating a valuation between 1.8 and 2 trillion dollars ahead of a roadshow targeted for the week of November 9th, though at least one research firm is sticking with a far more skeptical number.

ANDREW: Which tells you the valuation argument isn't settled just because the revenue number looked good.

JENNY: Exactly — strong growth, but the price tag is still very much a debate.

JENNY: There's also a new frontier model out this week. Google began broadly shipping Gemini 4 Argon, pitching it squarely at enterprise customers for long-horizon work like code migration, finance, law, and cybersecurity. Introductory pricing is two dollars per million input tokens and ten dollars per million output tokens, though that jumps to four and twenty after November 30th.

ANDREW: Worth watching whether banks and lenders start actually plugging that into their workflows, given everything we track on the mortgage side.

JENNY: Exactly the kind of adoption story we'll keep an eye on.

JENNY: One more to flag briefly. The AI-driven bank breach out of South Korea — reports now put the number of affected financial firms as high as sixteen, though that figure is only coming from one outlet so far. There's still no arrest, and the suspect CrowdStrike has pointed to continues to deny any involvement.

JENNY: Andrew, that inflation report had to be rippling through your other beat too.

ANDREW: It is, in a slightly counterintuitive way. Even with the ten year Treasury yield easing to around 5.1 percent after the report, the thirty year fixed mortgage rate actually ticked up, tracking around 7.45 to 7.46 percent according to Mortgage News Daily and Forbes' rate survey. Bankrate's own survey runs even higher, at 7.63 percent.

JENNY: So rates went up even though the Treasury yield went down?

ANDREW: Mortgage pricing doesn't move in lockstep with the ten year day to day. Lenders are also pricing in the Fed uncertainty we just talked about, and right now that's pushing rates the other direction. Freddie Mac's official weekly rate is due out later today — last week's reading was 7.40 percent, so we'll see if it catches up.

JENNY: What's that doing to people actually trying to get a loan right now?

ANDREW: It's thinning out demand. The Mortgage Bankers Association's latest weekly survey, for the week ending October 9th, showed applications down 2.7 percent. Purchase applications fell 4 percent, and refinancing applications are down 56 percent from a year ago — not surprising with rates near three year highs.

ANDREW: One more to watch on the regulatory side. FHFA Director Bill Pulte was expected to formally announce a shift away from the standard three bureau credit check toward a cheaper two bureau model at last week's mortgage bankers conference. That announcement still hasn't materialized, so for now it remains under consideration rather than official policy.

ANDREW: Jenny, what's the weather looking like down there today, and what's on your local beat?

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a high near 86 degrees today, mostly sunny with light winds. Enjoy it — News4Jax says a cold front moves in later this week and brings a windy weekend.

JENNY: On the local front, the JTA financial saga took another serious turn. The Florida Attorney General's office issued a third subpoena to the transit authority, this one ordering interim executive director Cleveland Ferguson to turn over records by October 30th. That subpoena specifically seeks communications involving Ferguson, former CEO Nat Ford, and Mayor Donna Deegan.

ANDREW: Wait, the mayor's office is now part of this?

JENNY: Her communications are part of what's being requested, yes — that doesn't mean she's accused of anything, but it shows how far this investigation has reached. Meanwhile, the City Council's new oversight committee, chaired by Council Member Chris Miller with Ron Salem as vice chair, is due to report back by December 4th.

ANDREW: So two tracks running at once — the council's internal review and the Attorney General's criminal-leaning probe.

JENNY: Exactly, and both converge in the next few weeks.

JENNY: On the utility side, JEA's new electric and water rate hikes have now been in effect two weeks, adding about 6 percent to electric bills and 8 percent to water and sewer bills. According to one report from News4Jax, the utility's next increase won't come until the 2027-28 budget year, tied to a new power plant costing an estimated 1.5 billion dollars. Jody Brooks remains interim CEO since late September, and the board is just now beginning to pick a search firm for a permanent replacement.

JENNY: And the downtown Publix tower incentive package, just shy of 50 million dollars, is still on hold. The package splits into a 21.4 million dollar grant tied to the project's future tax value and a 28.25 million dollar completion grant. The Finance Committee pushed its vote to November 4th, deliberately scheduled after next month's Amendment 3 election, given how much that ballot measure could affect the city's budget. If it clears committee, the full Council would vote November 10th.

JENNY: Andrew, before we go, what should we be watching?

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's fireside chat in Bangkok later today with the IMF's Kristalina Georgieva. It's his first public appearance since yesterday's hot inflation number, and markets will parse every word for a signal on the October 28th rate decision. Remember, hike odds spiked above 50 percent yesterday before settling back near 37. If Warsh sounds like Daly, hawkish, expect that number to climb again. If he sounds like Bowman, expect it to ease.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Thursday. Have a great day.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.
